name: Carlo De Franceschi
lead: Born at Moncalvo of modest landowners; elected to the Imperial Parliament in 1848, expelled from the judiciary in 1854, and the first serious historian of his own county.
record: as the Gologorica register writes it
Dominus Josephus de Franceschi and Lambertina née Peschle
Dominus Josephus Defranceschi, b. c.1722, d. 1782
Gymnasium-lyceum at Capodistria; earlier studies at Fiume and Gorizia
signed so, as a wedding witness in the Pisino marriage register, 13 September 1842
Deputy for Pisino, Imperial Constituent Parliament
Julius at Rovinj 1854; Lamberta and Aurelia Augusta at Poreč, July 1867; Virginia at Poreč 1876, aged 18
Lamberta carries his own mother's name. Inferred — the entries give the father only as Caroli
life: He is in his own parish register. The Gologorica books, read from microfilm held by the Pazin Records Office, give him as **Carolus Josephus Defranceschi**, born 17 October 1809 — the second of ten children of *Dominus Josephus de Franceschi* and *Lambertina née Peschle*, in house 17, recorded under the class *Civilis*. His parents had married on 3 February 1807. Every printed account says his mother came from Volosca; the census row beside her name says the same word.

The entry that fixes the generation above him is his elder brother's. Josephus Lambertus was baptised on 17 March 1808, and the register calls their father *“Dnus Josephus de Franceschi defuncti Josephi filius”* — son of the late Josephus. That joins the household to **Dominus Josephus Defranceschi** and his wife **Helena**, who appear through the 1760s and 1770s as godparents, and whose title marks what the family was in that village.

His biographer records him as born *da modesti possidenti* — of modest landowners. Not gentry, not armigerous, not the family a heraldry catalogue would sell you. That single phrase is worth more than any crest.

Back from Graz he joined a circle of young liberal intellectuals publishing the *Giornale critico politico* in secret, strongly anti-Austrian, while simultaneously serving in the Imperial-Royal magistrature — Italian being the official language of the courts in the Austro-Italian provinces. He was under police surveillance for years.

In 1848 he took part in the popular movement for a constitution and was elected deputy for Pisino, sitting with Michele Fachinetti, Antonio Madonizza, Francesco Vidulich and Giuseppe Vlach. Together they defeated the proposal to attach Istria to the German Confederation. His article *Per l'italianità dell'Istria*, published first in Vienna and then Trieste, became the manifesto of Istrian autonomism.

In 1854 the Austrian government threw him out of the judiciary, calling him a known apostle of Mazzini, an Istrian separatist and a provocateur. He moved to Fiume, and returned in 1861 for the *Dieta del Nessuno* at Parenzo — the session where Istrian deputies answered the roll call for Vienna with 'nobody'.

He then did the work he is remembered for: the province studied in its monuments, traditions, names, archaeology, ethnography and economy. He fed material to Pietro Kandler, wrote the *Statistica Agraria dell'Istria*, published through the appendices of the *Osservatore Triestino*, the weekly *Istria* and *La Provincia dell'Istria*, and in 1879 brought out *L'Istria: note storiche* at Parenzo.
source: Gologorica parish registers, Pazin Records Office microfilm ZM34K-214 and ZM34K-215

name: Camillo De Franceschi
lead: Carlo's youngest child. Imprisoned at twenty-one for a firecracker in a Trieste square; died in Venice, an exile, having written the standard history of the county his family came from.
record: German gymnasium at Pisino, then Trieste; Academy of Commerce, 1889
Two years, with a day of fasting and isolation every two months
life: His baptism is in the indexed Poreč register: *Camillo Romano Defranceschi*, born 3 August 1868, of Carlo Defranceschi and **Maria Michelcich**. Every printed account of him gives his mother as Maria *Micheli*. The register gives *Michelcich* — a Croatian surname in -ić, written the Austrian way. Somewhere between the font and the page, the mother of Istria's great Italian antiquarian was quietly Italianised out of her own name.

He was the last of Carlo's four children, and his father moved to Pisino to be near him while he attended the German gymnasium there. When the institute closed he finished school in Trieste and took a commerce degree in 1889.

From 1886 he was in the Julian Action Committee, distributing the clandestine *L'Eco dell'Alpe Giulia* and helping build a conspiracy network across Istria. On 24 March 1889 a committee of pro-Austrians tried to inaugurate a monument in Trieste's station square celebrating the city's devotion to the Habsburgs. The Action Committee left a firecracker there. A police inspector picked it up and injured his hand.

The arrests followed in September. At the trial, after five months of solitary confinement, the court described the accused as a society positively opposed to the present order of things. Camillo, at twenty-one the oldest of the group, got two years — six months more than the others — aggravated by a day of fasting and isolation every second month. He served it in the castle of Gradisca.

Released in February 1892, he reached home in time to help his father through his last months; Carlo died the following January. Attilio Hortis then found him a position at the municipal library in Trieste, and he spent the rest of his life in the archives.

His *Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino* — the largest and probably most important thing he wrote — was published in Venice in 1964, eleven years after his death, edited by his own son Carlo. He had died in Venice in 1953, an exile from the province he spent his life documenting.
works: Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino

name: Valentino Defranceschi
lead: Came from Carnia and was made a citizen of Fiume in 1739 — the same year he baptised a son there. Fourteen of his children are now recovered from the Rijeka register.
life: The existing family research records him as coming *from Carnia* — no parish named. Mione and Ovaro are in Carnia, and Carnian weavers and traders were moving into the Venetian and Habsburg Adriatic through exactly this period, so the identification is plausible and unproven in equal measure.

What is striking is the timing. Valentino was made a citizen of Fiume in 1739; Giovanni Battista Defranceschi arrived from the County of Pazin around 1740 and was made a citizen in 1746. Two men of the same surname, from the two regions this family claims, in the same port, within eighteen months. The existing research treats them as unrelated. That is an inference from an absent record, not a documented fact, and it is the most interesting question in this archive.

The Rijeka register carries the whole household. **Fourteen children** of Valentino and Helena — Elena — are recorded between 1737 and 1757, nine sons and five daughters. The received family account says he and Elena had ten sons and four daughters. Against an index that is only a quarter complete, that is as close to a match as this kind of evidence gets.

The dates line up with the citizenship exactly. Valentino was made a citizen of Fiume in 1739; his son Matheus Franciscus was baptised there on 17 September that same year, and a daughter, Josepha Catharina, had already been baptised on 26 November 1737. He was in the city and having children before the city formally took him in.

Five of the fourteen are recorded dying as infants — Mattio and Nicolo both in 1742, Antonio in 1753, Aloysia and Maria both in 1757. Two of those pairs died in the same year as each other, which in a port city usually means an epidemic rather than a coincidence.
source: FamilySearch, Croatia Church Books 1516–1994, Rijeka (Vitipolis / Fiume) entries

name: Giovanni Battista Defranceschi
lead: Came from the County of Pazin around 1740 and was made a citizen of Fiume in 1746.
life: Gologorica's baptism register opens in 1644 and runs unbroken through his likely birth years. The book that would name him is catalogued and sitting in the parish office in the village — undigitised, which is why this page still says *inferred*.

name: Domenico de Franceschi
lead: Recorded from 1614. The earliest of the three lines the existing research treats as unrelated.
record: Giovanni Paolo and Marco Antonio, municipal councillors in 1655
life: Details are sparse and the line disperses. Included because it is part of the received account and because anything that later joins it must be able to find it.

name: Zuane De Franceschi
lead: Named in 1679, with a son, as a weaver of Mione working in the Habsburg County of Pazin. The oldest documented tie between this family's two Italian-side origins.
record: list drawn up by the merighi, the village headmen
Mione, parish of Ovaro, Canale di Gorto
a son of his, and Zuane d'Erman of Mione
‘nell'Istria, luogo imperiale’ — the County of Pazin
life: The entry reads, in the headmen's own words: *da Mione «Zuane De Franceschi con un suo fiolo, Zuane d'Erman: questi tre nell'Istria, luogo imperiale»* — from Mione, Zuane De Franceschi with a son of his, and Zuane d'Erman: these three in Istria, an imperial place.

Three things in that one line matter. First, it is a De Franceschi *of Mione* — the surname is in the Carnian village, not merely near it. Second, *luogo imperiale* means the Habsburg County of Pazin specifically; the list only recorded men who went to imperial territory, because that is what the question asked, and Venetian Istria — where most Gorto emigrants actually went — was left out of the answers entirely. Third, he took a son.

The County of Pazin is where Gologorica and Gračišće are. It is the county Giovanni Battista Defranceschi is said to have left for Fiume around 1740, sixty-one years later, and the county in which the De Franceschi house on the Gologorica square was built in 1711, thirty-two years later.

This does not prove descent. It does move the Carnia–Istria link from a plausible story about weavers in general to a named man of this surname, from this village, in this county, on a dated list. Zuane d'Erman came from Mione too; the Erman were another Gorto weaving family, and their contracts survive in the Micoli Toscano family archive at Mione.
source: Elenco dei merighi, 1679, quoted in Dean Brhan, ‘Emigrazione della borghesia di montagna friulana dal Canale di Gorto in Istria’

name: Gaspar de Franceschi
lead: Recorded at Omiš in 1590 as owner of the warship Vascello and later admiral of the fleet. The family chart gives him dates, 1562–1609, and a wife.
life: Two independent accounts put a Gaspar de Franceschi at Omiš in 1590 with a warship and later the rank of admiral. The Omiš family chart adds the dates and the marriage, and places him eighth in a line reaching back to Zadar in the 1300s.
source: Maja Delić Peršen, ‘Obitelj de Franceschi u Imotskom od 1717. do danas’

name: Zuane Ivan Franceschi
lead: A landowner on the Omiš coast who took in six hundred refugees and kept them for two and a half years, then raised a company at his own expense, took the town of Imotski before the Venetian army arrived, was first through the wall of the fortress — and was ruined by it.
record: Giovanni il Zuane, 1673–1741, Colonnello Governatore; wife Francesca Cvitanović
Member of the town council of Omiš (Almissa)
Received 15 friars from the Prološko monastery, plus 200 families — some 600 people — and their livestock, at his estate at Dobrč, today Pisak
Sheltered them, and represented them to Alvise Mocenigo III, Provveditore Generale of Dalmatia
Raised and paid for a unit of 250 men
Took the varoš of Imotski before the main Venetian force arrived
First into the fortress behind the outer wall, where he raised the flag of St Mark
Named in General Emo's dispatch to the Doge
The begluk of arci-beg Čaušević — land, houses, a mill and a tower on the Vrljika — later called Perinuša
life: **The war he was caught in was not about him.** On 9 December 1714 the Ottoman Empire declared war on Venice, and inside a hundred days the Republic lost the whole Peloponnese, the great prize of the previous war. In July 1716 an Ottoman army landed on Corfu; the siege was lifted in August. Austria came in on Venice's side in April 1716 and won the battles that mattered — Petrovaradin, then Belgrade in 1717. Dalmatia was a sideshow of a sideshow: a mountain frontier where the pasha of Bosnia came down on Sinj in the summer of 1715 with a reputed forty thousand men and was thrown back. It is on that frontier, in that summer, that this family enters the record.

**January 1715: the refugees.** The Ottoman line ran within sight of the Franciscan house at Prološko blato. When it broke, fifteen friars and the people of the Imotski district went over the mountain and down to the sea. On 11 January 1715 Zuane Ivan Franceschi took the whole of it onto his own land at Dobrče — today Pisak, on the coast road below Omiš: the fifteen friars, about two hundred families, some six hundred people, and their livestock. They stayed until July 1717. Two and a half years of feeding, pasturing and defending a refugee camp on a private estate, in a war, with thieves working the coast. He also went to Alvise Mocenigo III, the Provveditore Generale of Dalmatia, and got them leave to build a monastery at Skalice in Omiš, where until then there had only been a chapel. That house carried the by-name *imotski* until the Imoćani went home.

**Nobody wanted the campaign.** Venice was exhausted and had lost the Morea; the Imotski *kadiluk* was of no strategic use to a republic whose priorities were now at sea. The push came from below — from the friars in exile, from the Omiš gentry, Franceschi and Caralipeo among them, and from a Mostar-born merchant, Šoić-Mirilović, who offered to pay for the artillery and to cover the loss of any gun, and put up a deposit in gold to make Mocenigo move. Only then did Mocenigo order Balbi and General Emo to raise an army.

**What it cost the brothers.** Three of them — Zuane Ivan, Frane and Matija — recruited a company of 250 men and carried the cost themselves. The state's money ran two months late and the rate was halved: ten soldi a day for a foot-soldier, down from twenty, and a piece of ship's biscuit. Fra Stipan Vrljić and fra Lovre Šitović raised the local volunteers, mostly Imoćani out of the refugee camp with some men from Sinj. Count Pavao Caralipeo brought the guns over roadless country on ox-teams as far as Zadvarje; from there the volunteers dragged them. Of the three brothers only Zuane went with the company as its commander.

**25 July 1717.** He took the *varoš* — the town below the rock — before the main force arrived. When Emo came up that evening with all his artillery he found the work already done, and said so to the Doge on 1 August: *«nakon što je Gov. Zuane Franceschi zauzeo varošicu…»*, after Governor Zuane Franceschi had taken the town. What was left was the fortress on the cliff above the lake, held by a garrison who refused the summons, provisioned for a siege, expecting relief from the thirty thousand Ottoman troops gathered in the Duvno plain — relief that never came, because their communications had been cut. The sappers went at the base of the rock. Somewhere in that, Zuane Ivan Franceschi went through the outer wall first and put the standard of St Mark on it.

**And then it destroyed him.** He had bankrupted himself on the campaign. The reward was the *begluk* of the arci-beg Čaušević on the Vrljika — a house, a Turkish tower, eight mills — and it was worthless when he got it: the district had fled, the mills barely turned, and grain could not cross a new and skirmishing frontier from the Bosnian hinterland. With nothing left he took a Venetian war galley, and off the Albanian coast near Durrës the Turkish galleys caught the fleet and destroyed it. He escaped on the flagship, which happened to carry the war chest — and saving the money is the only reason Venice did not imprison him for life for the loss of the ships. They interned him instead on his own estate at Pisak, forbidden to leave it. He never saw Omiš again and never returned to Imotski. He died at Pisak in 1741 and lies in the little church of St Mark, built in 1564, where his grave still is.

**The frontier he helped fix is still there.** The Treaty of Passarowitz of 21 July 1718 confirmed the Dalmatian gains, and the line drawn then is, with adjustments, the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina today. Imotski is in Croatia because of that summer. Of the seventy Venetians living in the town afterwards, only the de Franceschi settled and stayed.

**Two things survive of him that are not deeds.** One is a letter to his friend Dr Antonio Lubin, written after he had ridden round the freed district, describing the karst chasms above Imotski — *«Crven je to kamen, a nema na njemu ni mladice ni grma da pruže utjehu tim strahovitim liticama»*, it is red stone, with neither shoot nor shrub on it to comfort those fearful cliffs — printed long afterwards in the Zadar weekly *La Dalmazia* in 1846, and still one of the most vivid descriptions of that landscape anyone has written. The other is a song. Fra Andrija Kačić Miošić, a contemporary, put the taking of Imotski into the *Razgovor ugodni naroda slovinskoga* — the *Pismarica*, first printed 1756 and reprinted sixty-five times — in the folk decasyllable, to be sung to the gusle. He is in it. But he is in it under the wrong name.

**The name that was not his.** *Perinuša*, the estate, is not called after him or after any Franceschi. It is called after the **Perinović** — Perin — of Zadar, whom the family brought in at the start of the eighteenth century as stewards and overseers, and who followed them to their other properties. The by-name attached to the place, then to the owners, and so Kačić sings of the hero of Imotski as **«Perinović Ive»**. After 1945 the same confusion was used against the family, as evidence that the Franceschi were merely Italianised Perinovići and therefore not to be trusted; the two lines are distinct and the genealogy runs unbroken from the fourteenth century. The other standing slander — that an ancestor rode round the estate in a day and kept whatever he could enclose — is answered by the documents: the land was a *begluk* that had belonged to Ottoman lords for two centuries, and it was assigned in lieu of pay.

**Why almost nobody in Imotski knows this.** Because the story that took hold instead is that the Ottomans fled from a herd of cattle with candles tied to their horns, and that the town was freed by the friars and the people alone. A local historian working the Zadar and Omiš archives put it bluntly: the friars never repaid the memory of the man who housed them for two and a half years, and his part was deliberately pushed out of the account so that theirs should not be diminished. The Venetian dispatches say otherwise, and they were written the same week.
source: The narrative follows «Obitelj de Franceschi u Imotskom od 1717. do danas» (Poskok.info), built on Ante Ujević's «Imotska krajina», fra Karlo Jurišić's doctoral thesis of 1972, fra Andrija Nikić's work in the Zadar state archive, and the Zadar, Omiš and Franciscan holdings — with General Emo's dispatch of 1 August 1717 quoted there directly. The wider war from the standard accounts of the Ottoman–Venetian war of 1714–1718. The family chart gives him as «Giovanni il Zuane, 1673–1741, Colonnello Governatore», wife Francesca Cvitanović. Read September 2026.
